title: Elastic Potential Energy
short_intro: Elastic potential energy is the potential energy stored within an elastic body as a result of deformation, such as stretching or compressing. It arises from the conservative internal forces that oppose the deformation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of elastic energy, work done in stretching a wire, energy density, and basic numerical problems based on Hooke's law and Young's modulus.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed derivation of elastic potential energy per unit volume, strain energy in terms of elastic constants, and energy stored under complex stress-strain conditions.

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Elastic Energy
bullets: When an external force deforms an elastic body, work is done against the interatomic forces.
This work is stored within the material in the form of potential energy, termed elastic potential energy or strain energy.
Upon removal of the deforming force, this stored energy is completely recovered if the deformation remains within the elastic limit.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Density in a Stretched Wire
bullets: Energy density is defined as the elastic potential energy stored per unit volume of the deformed material.
It depends quadratically on the longitudinal strain or linearly on the square of stress divided by Young's modulus.
Expressed in SI units as joules per cubic metre (J/m³).

concept_notes.heading: Behavior under Cyclic Loading and Hysteresis
bullets: During loading and unloading cycles within the elastic limit, the energy stored is fully recovered.
If the deformation exceeds the elastic limit, permanent plastic deformation occurs, and some energy is dissipated as heat.
The area of the stress-strain hysteresis loop represents the thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle.

concept_notes.heading: Work Done in Stretching a Spring vs. Wire
bullets: For a helical spring, the displacement is macroscopic and measured in meters, governed by spring constant k.
For a uniform wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, the displacement is distributed throughout, governed by Young's modulus Y.
Both follow the fundamental quadratic relation U = ½ Fx where F is the restoring force and x is the extension.

derivations.title: Derivation of Elastic Potential Energy of a Stretched Wire
derivations.conditions: Uniform wire of original length L, cross-sectional area A, Young's modulus Y, stretched by an incremental extension x.
steps: According to Hooke's law, the tension F required to produce an extension x is given by F = \frac{YA}{L} x.
The small amount of work dW done in producing an additional infinitesimal extension dx is dW = F dx = \frac{YA}{L} x dx.
Integrating this work from zero to total extension l yields the total elastic potential energy U = \int_{0}^{l} \frac{YA}{L} x dx.
Solving the integral gives U = \frac{YA}{2L} l^2.

derivations.title: Derivation of Elastic Energy Density (Energy per Unit Volume)
derivations.conditions: Isotropic elastic medium undergoing longitudinal strain within the elastic limit.
steps: Start with the expression for total potential energy U = \frac{1}{2} \frac{YA}{L} l^2.
Divide the total energy by the volume of the wire V = A \times L to obtain energy density u.
Recognize that \frac{Y l}{L} is stress (σ) and \frac{l}{L} is strain (ε).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force versus Extension Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a F-x Cartesian plot, ending within the elastic limit.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the line represents the stiffness constant (YA/L or k). The area enclosed under the line with the displacement axis represents the total elastic potential energy stored.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested for calculating work done or comparing energy storage capacities of different wires or springs.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stress-Strain Curve and Elastic Energy Storage
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A standard stress-strain curve showing the proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, and fracture point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the curve up to the elastic limit gives the resilience or maximum elastic energy density the material can store without permanent damage.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to distinguish between resilience, toughness, and proof stress in conceptual PGT questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus / Young's Modulus Energy Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing reference and experimental wires, spirit level, micrometer screw gauge, and added load weights.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measurement of extension corresponding to known incremental loads allows experimental verification of the work-energy relations in stretched metallic wires.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical physics principle adapted for objective numerical evaluation.

solved_numericals.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 mm² is stretched by 1 mm. If Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m², calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 2 m, A = 1.0 mm² = 1.0 × 10&sup-;&sup6; m², l = 1 mm = 1.0 × 10&sup-;³ m, Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
Substitute values into the formula U = \frac{YA l^2}{2L}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the energy density stored in a copper wire subject to a longitudinal stress of 4 × 10&sup7; N/m². Given Young's modulus for copper is 1.2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Stress σ = 4 × 10&sup7; N/m², Y = 1.2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
Use the energy density formula in terms of stress: u = \frac{\sigma^2}{2Y}.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform elastic spring of force constant 500 N/m is stretched by 5 cm from its natural length. Calculate the potential energy stored in the spring.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: k = 500 N/m, x = 5 cm = 0.05 m.
Use the spring potential energy formula: U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Valid strictly within the elastic limit where Hooke's law is obeyed and no permanent plastic deformation occurs.

Assumes the material is homogeneous, isotropic, and its cross-sectional area remains nearly constant during stretching (neglecting lateral contraction governed by Poisson's ratio for basic calculations).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Elastic potential energy stored in a wire is directly proportional to the total length of the wire.
common_misconceptions.correct: Energy density is independent of length, and total energy for a given extension is inversely proportional to the original length (U ∝ 1/L).
common_misconceptions.why: Longer wires offer less stiffness (k = YA/L) for the same cross-sectional area, reducing the restoring force for a given extension l.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Work done in stretching a wire equals Force times Extension (F × l).
common_misconceptions.correct: Work done equals one-half of the product of Force and Extension (½ F l).
common_misconceptions.why: The force increases linearly from zero to F as the extension increases from zero to l, requiring integration or the average force.

quick_revision: Elastic energy formula: U = ½ F l = \frac{YA l^2}{2L}.
Elastic Potential Energy of a Wire: U = \frac{YA l^2}{2L}
